meaning: Son of the Aśvins and Mādrī — twin of Nakula, youngest of the Pāṇḍu princes, famed for wisdom

phonemes.desc: Short a; the prefix sa- means “with” — Sahadeva, “god with god”.
The h is a light aspirate; the compound honours the twin-born’s doubled divinity.
“God”: the name is a sentence — a god attended by gods.

kin.label: Epic epithet
kin.form: the wisest of the Pāṇḍavas after Yudhiṣṭhira — the astronomer

pronunciation.note: Youngest of the Pāṇḍavas, famed for wisdom, astrology, and the sword — the quiet savant of the five.

domains.title: Twin of Nakula, Famed for Wisdom
domains.subtitle: The Youngest Pāṇḍava, the Astronomer
domains.lead: Sahadeva is the youngest Pāṇḍava: twin of Nakula, son of the Aśvin physicians, and the epic’s scholar-warrior — master of astrology and the calendar, keeper of the sword-skills that matched his twin’s, and the brother whose advice was always right and rarely heeded. Yudhiṣṭhira named him the wisest of the five; the war’s chronology ran by his stars.

cards.name: The Astronomer
cards.desc: His knowledge of the stars set the war’s calendar; the epic calls his astrology infallible.

cards.name: The Sword
cards.desc: His blade-work equalled Nakula’s — the twins were the epic’s matched pair of arms.

cards.name: The Cattle-Seer
cards.desc: Like his twin he knew herds — but Sahadeva read their breeding and their futures too.

cards.name: The Unheeded Counsel
cards.desc: He advised the dice-refusal and the war’s conduct — right, and passed over.

mythology.lead: Sahadeva’s mythology is the epic’s study of wisdom without power: the youngest brother whose knowledge was perfect and whose influence was nil. He knew the dice-game was ruin, the war’s timing, the omens’ meaning — and the epic lets him speak each truth once, then moves on. His death on the mountain was for the one pride knowledge permits: the pride of being right.

myths.title: The Younger Twin
myths.text: Mādrī called the Aśvin twins and bore two sons — Nakula first, Sahadeva second — both radiant as the gods. Orphaned at the funeral pyre that took Mādrī, the twins were raised by Kuntī as her own: the youngest of five, the astronomer among warriors, born with the physician-gods’ second sight.

myths.title: The Counsel Against the Dice
myths.text: When the challenge to the dice-game came, Sahadeva — who had calculated the stars and the odds — advised refusal to the last. The epic notes that the advice was heard and overridden; the fall of the Pāṇḍavas into thirteen years of loss begins at the moment the youngest brother’s arithmetic is outvoted.

myths.title: Tantripala the Cowherd
myths.text: In the incognito year he served Virāṭa as Tantripala, keeper of the cattle — and the herds multiplied under his accounting. The disguise-book’s joke runs deepest here: the astronomer disguised as a cowherd ran the kingdom’s true prosperity while the king praised his other servants.

myths.title: The Pride of the Right
myths.text: On the final mountain, Sahadeva fell second — and Yudhiṣṭhira named his sin: ‘he thought none his equal in wisdom’. The epic’s most quietly devastating verdict: even the love of being right is a weight, and the wisest of the five carried his wisdom as others carried vanity.

lore.syncretism: Sahadeva is the Aśvins’ second son — the epic’s accounting keeps the physician-gods’ line in the heroic blood — and later tradition made him the type of the jyotiṣika, the court astrologer whose charts rule kingdoms. The twins together became the subcontinent’s archetype of matched excellence in different keys: Nakula the body’s arts, Sahadeva the mind’s.
lore.culturalLegacy: The twins’ names remain a matched set in Indian naming — Sahadeva a standing boy’s name meaning ‘attended by gods’. His unheeded-counsel scene is the epic’s image of every expert ignored by power; and the jyotiṣa tradition claims him as its founding hero, the astronomer inside the world’s longest poem.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sahadeva: ‘god with god’ — the name is a theology of twins. Restored plainly, it keeps the epic’s quietest lesson: wisdom that cannot persuade is still wisdom, and the stars he read were right whether the court listened or not. Four syllables, infallible and ignored.
lore.archaeology: As with Nakula, his monuments are the epic’s performance traditions and the Pāṇḍava-ratha reliefs of the Pallava south. The jyotiṣa-manuscript traditions of medieval India invoke his name as patron of the astronomical arts.
lore.cult: The Pāṇḍava-brotherhood village cults of the western Himalaya worship the set; astrologers’ lineages invoke him in their initiation verses. His festival is the epic-recitation itself.
lore.iconography: The twin beside Nakula, differentiated by the astrolabe or the chart in later paintings; his icon is the star-diagram — the heavens reduced to the hand.
lore.reception: Literary criticism reads Sahadeva as the Mahābhārata’s Cassandra — the truth-teller structurally fated to be ignored. In the study of expertise and power, his scenes are cited as the epic’s analysis of how organizations fail: the one who calculates best is the one the assembly interrupts.
